passage: An hour before the call with Noor, Seema had her slides ready: the cause, the new date, the recovery steps. Then she remembered the last three meetings. Noor had put every question to Rajiv, the delivery head, and given Seema only a polite nod. "The message is fine," Seema thought. "The messenger isn't the person Noor trusts. That isn't about my ego. It's about whether Noor stays open to the plan." She rang Rajiv, who was stuck in a taxi. "Can you join and lead, and I'll cover the details?" "I'll be there in twenty minutes," he said. On the call Rajiv gave the news in two sentences. Noor listened, then asked, "And what's the plan?" Seema shared her slides.

qa.q: How long before the call was Seema's preparation ready?
qa.a: Seema had her slides ready an hour before the call.

qa.q: What did Seema realise while thinking about the last three meetings?
qa.a: Seema realised Noor trusted Rajiv most and might stay open to the news only if he led, and she put her ego aside.

qa.q: What else could Seema do to help Rajiv lead well, and why?
qa.a: Seema could send Rajiv the key points and the recovery steps before he joins, because the person leading needs the facts to hand.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Rajiv opens the call?
qa.a: Noor probably feels reassured to hear the news from someone trusted, which makes it easier to listen to the recovery plan.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: delegating the message to the person with the relationship [Thinking]
passage:
Gargi stared at the draft email in the co-working space in Koramangala and didn't press send.
The logistics client's launch was three weeks late. She had the recovery plan ready. But she kept thinking about last quarter's review, where the client's owner, Mr. Bhalla, had barely looked at her and had spent twenty minutes joking with Chaitanya about cricket.
"He trusts Chaitanya," she said under her breath. "If I send this cold, he reads it as another vendor excuse. If Chaitanya opens the call, he'll actually listen to the plan."
She walked to Chaitanya's desk. "Can you lead Friday's call with Bhalla? I'll handle the details."
Chaitanya raised an eyebrow, then nodded. "Leave the opening to me," he said.
On Friday, Bhalla grumbled for two minutes, then said, "Okay, Chaitanya, walk me through what you're doing." Gargi shared the plan, and he asked good questions.

qa.q: Where was Gargi when she decided not to send the email?
qa.a: She was at the co-working space in Koramangala.

qa.q: Why did Gargi hesitate to send the email herself?
qa.a: She was worried Mr. Bhalla would read a cold email from her as another excuse, because at the last review he barely looked at her and clearly trusted Chaitanya.

qa.q: What else could Gargi have done if Chaitanya had been unavailable on Friday?
qa.a: She could have met Bhalla in person with the plan, explained the cause plainly and set a regular update rhythm, so he could judge the recovery himself.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Gargi's request?
qa.a: He may feel trusted and a little surprised to be asked to lead, and he can see she is putting the client relationship ahead of her own credit.

grounding: It shows an account lead reasoning that the client trusts the delivery head most and asking him to lead the talk, which keeps the client open to the recovery plan.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: delegating the message to the person with the relationship [Thinking]
passage:
"The Kolkata client won't take this well from me," Mohit said, rubbing his forehead.
"Why not? You're the account lead," Uday said, closing his laptop in the small meeting room.
"Because every time there's a problem, Mrs. Ganguly asks for you. You ran her first rollout. She calls you 'the one who fixed the billing mess'."
"That was two years ago."
"Exactly. Two years of trust. If I tell her the data module slips by a month, she'll hear a stranger making promises. If you tell her, she'll hear someone who's delivered before."
Uday was quiet. "And then what? I just read your plan?"
"No. You open, you explain, you ask her what worries her most. I'll take the details."
"Fine. Book the call."
The next day, Mrs. Ganguly sighed loudly, then said, "Uday, tell me honestly. Is this plan real?" He said yes, and she asked for the timeline.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Ganguly call Uday?
qa.a: She called him "the one who fixed the billing mess".

qa.q: What was Mohit worried about when he rubbed his forehead?
qa.a: He was worried that Mrs. Ganguly would hear bad news from him as promises from a stranger and lose confidence, because she trusts Uday more.

qa.q: Which approach might suit Mohit better if he wanted to build his own relationship with Mrs. Ganguly over time?
qa.a: He could join the call with Uday, handle the details himself and then send the regular updates, so she starts to link him with reliable follow-through.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Mrs. Ganguly when Uday leads the call?
qa.a: Hearing it from someone who has delivered before, she feels able to ask honestly whether the plan is real and then moves on to the timeline instead of shutting down.

grounding: It shows an account lead realising the client trusts the delivery head most and asking him to lead the difficult call, which keeps the client open to the plan.
